items.stem: A shopper presses Submit twice on a form that sends `POST /enrollments`. What will the table hold after two identical POST requests?

options.text: Two new rows, because every POST creates a new item
options.feedback: POST is not idempotent. The server treats each POST as a new request and creates a new item every time, even when the body is identical.

options.text: One row, because the second request is identical to the first
options.feedback: The server does not compare requests. Each POST creates something new, so identical requests still produce duplicates.

options.text: One row, because the server rejects duplicates automatically
options.feedback: Servers reject duplicates only if you build that rule (for example a unique constraint or an idempotency key). Nothing in POST itself prevents them.

items.try: In the step "Send a request", press Send with POST selected, then Send the same one again, and count the rows.

items.stem: An edit form sends `PATCH /courses/ITENT45` with the body `{"units": 6}`. Because of network problems the same request reaches the server three times. What is the course's `units` value afterward?

options.text: 6, because every request writes the same value and leaves other fields alone
options.feedback: PATCH sets the fields in the body to the given values. Repeating it writes the same value again, so PATCH here is idempotent.

options.text: 18, because each of the three requests added 6 units to the course
options.feedback: PATCH with a plain value replaces the field. Only a request written as an increment, such as 'add 6 units', would add up, and that kind of request would not be idempotent.

options.text: 6, but the second and third requests also create two extra courses
options.feedback: Creating new items is what POST does. PATCH changes an existing item and does not create anything.

options.text: The title and slots are cleared, because the body left them out of the request
options.feedback: That describes PUT. PATCH leaves fields that are not in the body untouched.

items.stem: Select all that apply. Which of these statements about status codes are correct?

options.text: 401 means the server does not know who you are.
options.feedback: 401 is named Unauthorized and means unauthenticated. Sending login details and trying again can fix it.

options.text: 403 means the server knows who you are and still refuses.
options.feedback: Better credentials will not help, because the user is not allowed to do this.

options.text: 500 means the URL names nothing, so check the path and the id.
options.feedback: That describes 404. A 500 means the server code failed with an error while handling the request.

options.text: 404 means the server code raised an error while handling the request.
options.feedback: That describes 500. A 404 means the URL names nothing, so check the path and the id.
